blocks.text: Self-taught photographer and filmmaker Shayan Sajadian has won the 20th Foam Paul Huf Award for images that offer a view of Iran’s forgotten, “neither sensational nor nostalgic.”
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Shayan Sajadian .

Shayan Sajadian was born in Shiraz in 1994. There he studied architecture at the University of Art and Architecture, buying a camera to document his fieldwork: façades, alleyways, the geometry of Persian urban space. Nothing in that training prepared him for portraiture, which he taught himself. It was in the old neighborhoods of the city’s south, however, that one encounter changed everything.

There he stumbled upon a neighborhood of homeless people and drug users. The scene shook him. He kept going back — to those cut off from their families, their communities, their state by heroin and crystal meth, and then to the dealers too. “Photography,” he says, “has always been a magical, unexpected experience for me — a way of stepping outside the safety of my bubble.” Now based in Tehran, he has extended his gaze across the whole country.

He works over the long haul: talking at length, earning trust, never pressing the shutter until he has won real closeness. Some of his subjects end up posing on their own terms. The series Madness , Balochs , and State of Being — where tattooed men pass beneath streetlights — span four years. But since the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, arrested by the morality police in 2022, and Iran’s entry into war last February, raising a camera in the street has become a perilous act.

On November 12, 2026, at Paris Photo, an international jury chaired by Ethiopian photographer Aïda Muluneh honored his courage by awarding him the Foam Paul Huf Award. Founded in 2007 by Amsterdam’s photography museum Foam, the prize recognizes all photographic genres. Shayan Sajadian was selected from 105 candidates. “Shayan’s work offers us a different view of Iran,” the jury wrote, “one that moves beyond the political imagery and familiar narratives through which the country is so often represented. Although the photographs explore masculinity, there is a sense of tenderness within them.” The award comes with a €20,000 prize, a publication in Foam Magazine, and a solo exhibition at the museum in autumn 2027.
